Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: Elias Vance was fourteen when the compound walls fell. He does not recall a timeline, only the sudden, deafening cracks that tore through the courtyard, followed by a suffocating stillness. For days, he and his family huddled in a basement, where the absence of sound made every distant boot step sound like an executioner's approach, and unusual silences made him feel certain something dangerous was about to happen. When they finally crossed borders, the visual fragments of the attack-shattered doors, blood on stone, the way neighbors had fallen-burned behind his eyelids. Elias still felt his shoulders knot in the exact rigid posture he had held while crouching in that dark room, and sometimes, without any picture at all, the full emotional intensity of those nights would wash over him, leaving his chest tight and his breath shallow. Years later, settled in a quiet American suburb, Elias had trained himself into the demanding rhythm of a public defender. Because he had come to believe the world was fundamentally unsafe, his mind automatically began scanning for the visual echoes of that attack. Whenever he opened a heavy file folder or flipped through case evidence, the pages would momentarily become doorframes, and the old images would flood his vision, forcing his body to tense as if the violence were returning. These intrusive pictures did not stay passive; they immediately hijacked his nervous system. The moment a memory surfaced, his pulse would spike, his shoulders would rise to his ears, and ordinary office noises-a stapler snapping, a phone ringing-would trigger a violent startle, making him lurch back in his chair as though a weapon had just been drawn. The physiological alarms quickly dictated his daily behavior. The constant false alarms and sudden startles caused him to stop speaking about the event or its aftermath and to meticulously monitor his own thoughts for signs of going crazy. His partner, Maya, noticed how he flinched whenever a door closed too quietly in their apartment, and how he would constantly audit his mental space for cracks in his composure. This hyperawareness only made the threat response worse; the longer he avoided reminders by steering clear of others' questions, the more his body treated the present as a continuation of the past. The unrelenting startle responses actively pulled the worst visual memories forward, which in turn convinced him that the world was fundamentally hostile. By his second year on the job, the cycle had calcified into a rigid architecture. Elias's conviction that danger was omnipresent drove him to rigidly monitor his thoughts and steer clear of any conversation that might drift toward vulnerability. Meanwhile, the false alarms in his courtroom routine-shouting clients, slamming gavels, the sudden silence before a verdict-kept his threat system firing, which automatically pulled the worst visual memories forward, making his legs feel leaden and his vision tunnel. Each startle response fed directly back into his negative appraisals, reinforcing the certainty that he had to be on guard at all times and stay especially careful because he never knew what could happen next. The more he watched his own mind for cracks, the more certain he became that the past was still actively hunting him. This avoidance, in turn, starved his brain of corrective experiences, leaving the belief that the world remained hostile entirely unchallenged. The breaking point arrived on a Tuesday, when a junior associate's dropped briefcase triggered a full-body freeze in the hallways of the federal courthouse, causing Elias to drop his own evidence packets and stumble backward until he could press himself against the wall. Maya found him there, breathing through a panic that felt identical to the basement, and told him he needed outside support. He finally agreed, not because the fear had lessened, but because he realized his attempts to outrun it had only tightened the trap. He sits in his first appointment now, bracing for the therapist's questions, terrified that confronting the memories will unleash the same relentless danger he has been fighting for seven years.
